articles.title: Registration is now full for the 2024 ERP Boot Camp
articles.content:
The demand for the 2024 ERP Boot Camp was far beyond our expectations, and we reached our maximum registration of 30 people within one day. We already have a waiting list of over 30 people, so we have closed the registration site.

We realize that this is very disappointing to many people. We hope to offer another workshop like this next summer, or possibly earlier.

If you would like to get announcements about upcoming boot camps and webinars, you should join our email list.

You may also consider hosting a Mini ERP Boot Camp at your institution (in person or over Zoom).

articles.title: New Paper: Using Multivariate Pattern Analysis to Increase Effect Sizes for ERP Amplitude Comparisons
articles.content:
Carrasco, C. D., Bahle, B., Simmons, A. M., & Luck, S. J. (2024). Using multivariate pattern analysis to increase effect sizes for event-related potential analyses. Psychophysiology, 61, e14570. https://doi.org/10.1111/psyp.14570 [preprint]

Multivariate pattern analysis (MVPA) can be used to “decode” subtle information from ERP signals, such as which of several faces a participant is perceiving or the orientation that someone is holding in working memory (see this previous blog post). This approach is so powerful that we started wondering whether it might also give us greater statistical power in more typical experiments where the goal is to determine whether an ERP component differs in amplitude across experimental conditions. For example, might we more easily be able to tell if N400 amplitude is different between two different classes of words by using decoding? If so, that might make it possible to detect effects that would otherwise be too small to be significant.

To address this question, we compared decoding with the conventional ERP analysis approach with using the 6 experimental paradigms in the ERP CORE. In the conventional ERP analysis, we measured the mean amplitude during the standard measurement window from each participant in the two conditions of the paradigm (e.g., faces versus cars for N170, deviants versus standards for MMN). We quantified the magnitude of the difference between conditions using Cohen’s dz (the variant of Cohen’s d corresponding to a paired t test). For example, the effect size in the conventional ERP comparison of faces versus cars in the N170 paradigm was approximately 1.7 (see the figure).

We also applied decoding to each paradigm. For example, in the N170 paradigm, we trained a support vector machine (SVM) to distinguish between ERPs elicited by faces and ERPs elicited by cars. This was done separately for each subject, and we converted the decoding accuracy into Cohen’s dz so that it could be compared with the dz from the conventional ERP analysis. As you can see from the bar labeled SVM in the figure above, the effect size for the SVM-based decoding analysis was almost twice as large as the effect size for the conventional ERP analysis. That’s a huge difference!

We found a similar benefit for SVM-based decoding over conventional ERP analyses in 7 of the 10 cases we tested (see the figure below). In the other 3 cases, the ERP and SVM effects were approximately equivalent. So, there doesn’t seem to be a downside to using decoding, at least in terms of effect size. But there can be a big benefit.

Because decoding has many possible benefits, we’ve added it into ERPLAB Toolbox. It’s super easy to use, and we’ve created detailed documentation and a video to explain how it works at a conceptual level and to show you how to use it.

We encourage you to apply it to your own data. It may give you the power to detect effects that are too small to be detected with conventional ERP analyses.

articles.title: Classic and novel features of the dentate gyrus vascular niche quantified through 3D vessel reconstruction
articles.content: Adult neurogenesis, the continued generation of new neurons throughout life, supports a variety of emotional and cognitive functions in mammals. Lifelong neurogenesis occurs in the dentate gyrus (DG) of the hippocampus, where a neurogenic niche supports the survival and growth of neural stem cells (NSCs), which divide to generate new neurons. A key component of this niche is the surrounding vasculature, thought to give NSCs access to circulating support molecules, oxygen, and nutrient metabolites. The DG vasculature is strikingly variable across layers. Vascular density and linearity, for example, have been noted to differ substantially in the different cell layers that make up the DG. Most of these prior descriptions of the DG vasculature have been qualitative, and other important aspects of vessel morphology, like vessel diameter, have not been previously reported to our knowledge. To provide a more complete and quantitative description of the adult DG vasculature, we used a 3D imaging technique to fully characterize the vasculature of each DG cellular layer. Our 3D reconstructions of DG blood vessels provide a quantitative method for measuring several known, qualitative features of the neurogenic niche, such as blood vessel density and tortuosity. In some cases, we reproduce qualitative observations, such as affirming that vessel density is high in the subgranular zone (SGZ) where NSCs reside and low in the granule cell layer. In other cases, our findings go counter to what qualitative observations suggest. For example, the SGZ is often described as having uniquely linear blood vessels, but we found that linearity was similar between the SGZ and hilus layer. We also report new measures of features of DG layer vascular architecture: vessel diameter and branching. Together, these findings offer a global, quantitative characterization of the DG vascular niche in adult mice. Beyond providing more detailed characterization of DG vasculature, we also anticipate our methods and estimates of variance in mice will be useful for investigators wishing to plan their own quantitative studies of changes in the vascular structure of the DG.
articles.author: Carter, I., Smith, B. M., Kirby, E. D.

articles.title: Nanoscale remodeling of synaptic glutamate receptors and calcium channels in temporal lobe epilepsy
articles.content: Temporal lobe epilepsy (TLE) is the most common form of focal epilepsy and remains drug-resistant in approximately one-third of patients, for whom surgical resection of the epileptogenic zone is currently the most effective treatment option. One strategy to improve therapeutic outcomes involves identifying the molecular mechanisms and key regulators underlying synaptic function. Although altered glutamatergic neurotransmission is considered a major contributor to epileptic hyperexcitability, the nanoscale organization of key synaptic proteins in the human epileptic cortex is still not well characterized. In particular, it remains unclear whether pre- and postsynaptic proteins undergo synapse-type-specific remodeling in TLE. Here, we used high-resolution freeze-fracture replica immunolabeling to map the nanoscale organization of postsynaptic AMPA receptors (AMPARs) and presynaptic P/Q-type voltage-gated calcium channels (CaV2.1) in glutamatergic synapses of cortical layers II/III of surgically resected human tissue. We examined perilesional, cytologically unremarkable, non-epileptogenic cortical tissue obtained from patients undergoing tumor resection (52-63 years; two female and three male patients) and compared these data with cortical samples from patients with refractory TLE (22-53 years; two female and four male patients). To assess whether pathological remodeling differs across synapse populations, we analyzed both excitatory dendritic spine and shaft synapses. We found a robust, highly consistent increase in AMPAR density at both spine and shaft synapses in TLE patients indicating enhanced postsynaptic excitatory signaling. However, AMPAR spatial reorganization differed between synapse types. Monte Carlo simulations demonstrated that spine synapses largely preserved a random receptor distribution without a significant clustering pattern, whereas shaft synapses exhibited a redistribution from clustering toward random receptor arrangements together with reduced center-preference within the postsynaptic density. In contrast, presynaptic CaV2.1 remodeling was more variable and predominantly associated with excitatory spine synapses. TLE spine synapses exhibited an overall increase in CaV2.1 density together with significantly larger and more numerous CaV2.1 nanoclusters within the active zone. This difference was particularly pronounced in male patients. In comparison, shaft synapses displayed only minor presynaptic alterations. CaV2.1 channels remained highly clustered under both control and epileptic conditions, indicating preservation of core active-zone organizational features despite disease-associated nanoscale remodeling. Together, these findings provide direct ultrastructural support that pathological plasticity in human TLE involves an overall increase in excitatory postsynaptic responsiveness and a target cell-specific increase of excitatory release probability at cortical synapses.
articles.author: Kaufmann, W. A., Venturino, A., Kleindienst, D., Roessler, K., Czech, T., Janssen, J. M., Engelhardt, M., Stefanits, H., Watanabe, M., Siegert, S., Shigemoto, R.

articles.title: Limb-localized induction of regeneration reshapes brain and amputation-site transcriptional states in adult Xenopus laevis
articles.content: Limb regeneration requires coordinated tissue reconstruction and nervous system reintegration, yet whether regenerative induction alters brain responses to limb loss remains unclear. We analyzed transcriptomics from the paired brains and amputation sites of adult Xenopus laevis after hindlimb amputation with or without a 24 hour exposure to localized, pro-regenerative multi-drug treatment (MDT) delivered through a wearable bioreactor device. At 24 hours post treatment (24 HPT), MDT brains showed increased vascular and basement membrane transcripts and enrichment of oxidative phosphorylation and mTORC1 programs. In the limb, an exploratory integrated stress response (ISR) score increased at 11 and 24 HPT and returned to control levels by 7 days post-treatment (7 DPT), coinciding with induction of growth differentiation factor 15 (GDF15), a cytokine responsive to mitochondrial stress. We detected no corresponding increase in brain ISR score. At 7 DPT, MDT brains showed enrichment of immune, heme metabolism and biosynthetic programs, reduced synaptic transmission gene expression, and increased gdf15.L. Relative to an external uninjured reference, MDT and amputation only brains showed concordant changes, with treatment modifying selected programs. Cross-species comparative analyses identified partial overlap with an axolotl regenerative glutamatergic signature and separation from selected mammalian injury profiles. These findings reveal cross-tissue responses to regenerative induction and identify candidate mechanisms of brain body communication in biomedically engineered vertebrate limb regeneration.
articles.author: Murugan, N. J., Russell, S., Kaplan, D., Levin, M., Miller, K.

articles.title: Muscarinic signaling sustains delay-period selectivity in prefrontal cortex by preserving thalamic drive
articles.content: Short-term memory (STM) requires the temporary maintenance of task-relevant information in prefrontal cortex (PFC). Reciprocal interactions between the mediodorsal thalamus (MD) and PFC have been implicated in sustaining this activity, but how thalamofrontal communication is maintained despite the biophysical constraints of repetitive synaptic transmission remains unclear. Here, we show that MD--PFC synapses exhibit profound frequency-dependent short-term depression, causing repetitive thalamic input to progressively lose its ability to drive PFC neurons. During STM performance, acetylcholine (ACh) levels in PFC rose rapidly following cue presentation and remained elevated throughout the delay period. Muscarinic ACh receptor (mAChR) activation did not alleviate synaptic depression, but instead increased the intrinsic excitability of PFC neurons, thereby preserving their responsiveness to weakened thalamic input. Conversely, mAChR blockade impaired STM performance and progressively disrupted delay-period directional representations at both the single-neuron and population levels, while largely sparing initial encoding. These findings identify muscarinic signaling as a postsynaptic gain mechanism that compensates for declining thalamofrontal efficacy and sustains task-relevant prefrontal representations during STM.
articles.author: Kim, Y., Kim, J., Choi, I. S., Lee, J., Yang, Y.-S., Choi, J. H., Choi, J.-W., Rah, J.-C.

articles.title: Engineered proteins to restore and enhance neurotransmitter release
articles.content: Synapse dysfunction is a hallmark feature of many neurological diseases. Synaptic transmission is initiated in nerve terminals, where active zone protein complexes control vesicle fusion for neurotransmitter release. Here, we engineer proteins that mediate active zone functions and demonstrate their use for reconstituting and strengthening neurotransmission. A protein composed of CaV{beta}4 and the RIM1 zinc finger, {beta}4-Zn, restored neurotransmitter release after active zone disruption through recruitment of Munc13. We develop {beta}4-MC, derived from the Munc13-1 MUN and C2C domains, which bypasses Munc13 recruitment and directly mediates vesicle docking, priming and fusion after active zone disruption. In {beta}4-MC, MUN domain functions are dispensable for docking, but active MUN and C2C domains are both necessary for neurotransmitter release. In wild-type mouse and human neurons, {beta}4-MC but not {beta}4-Zn strengthens neurotransmitter release. Furthermore, {beta}4-Zn and {beta}4-MC restore and enhance dopamine release in the mouse striatum, respectively. Hence, {beta}4 proteins are engineered secretory proteins with therapeutic potential as enhancers of synaptic function.
articles.author: Chin, M., Yang, K., Lopez, R. C., Tan, C., Kaeser, P. S.

articles.title: A genome-wide catalog of sites where peripheral DNA methylation reflects the brain
articles.content: Epigenetic studies of psychiatric and neurological disorders rely largely on peripheral tissues, yet where peripheral DNA methylation (DNAm) reflects the brain remains unclear. We generated a paired brain and peripheral DNAm dataset from 148 donors in three cohorts and combined it with five published cohorts for consensus brain-peripheral correlations. By cross-validation across cohorts, we defined brain epigenome shared sites (BrESS), more than 100,000 CpGs per tissue at which peripheral DNAm reproducibly predicts brain DNAm. BrESS lay at promoters active in both brain and periphery and in housekeeping genes, and most were not explained by genetic effects. BrESS did not contribute to the heritability of seven disorders, and CpGs from epigenome-wide association studies of these disorders were not enriched at BrESS. Peripheral DNAm reflects the brain mainly in a regulatory compartment shared across tissues, outside which disease signals largely lie, and BrESS separate peripheral signals attributable to the brain from others.

articles.title: Sound-Driven Motion of Human Cochlear Structures Depends on Organ of Corti Integrity
articles.content: Optical coherence tomography (OCT) was used to image and measure the passive sound-driven displacements of cochlear structures in situ through the intact round window membrane of fresh human cadaveric specimens at 12 to 30 hours postmortem. We find that the anatomical integrity of the organ of Corti (OoC) affects cochlear structural motion. OoC with high integrity (erect with supporting cells) have small osseous spiral lamina (OSL) motion. Conversely, OoC with low integrity (flattened without supporting cells) have large OSL motion. For the ratio of motion between the basilar membrane (BM) and OSL (BM/OSL), OoC with high integrity has large BM/OSL motion while a cochlear partition without OoC has small BM/OSL motion. Furthermore, the high-integrity OoC has reticular lamina surface motion that is lower than the BM, whereas low-integrity OoC has similar reticular lamina and BM motion. This relationship between OoC anatomical integrity and cochlear structural motion will have consequential effects on sound transduction.
articles.author: Secchia, P., McHugh, C. I., Cho, N. H., Zosuls, A., Tubelli, A., Puria, S., Nakajima, H. H.
